_comment: Canonical domain vocabulary for the Knowledge Graphs course. Most entries were harvested by shared/domain/harvest.py from the .term-tooltip definitions already written into output/*.html, so the wording is the course's own; the rest cover words the course uses constantly and defined nowhere. The runtime never touches an existing .term-tooltip, so the hand-written ones still win where they appear. Rebuild with shared/domain/build.py after anything that regenerates a module page.
title: Course Glossary
subtitle: Every domain word this course uses. Press g from anywhere.

glossary.short: Architecture Decision Records: short documents capturing a significant design decision, its context, and its consequences.
glossary.long: orderflow's docs/adr-001-event-bus.md is one.

glossary.short: The pipeline found more than one candidate and refused to guess.
glossary.long: The tag that matters most: a graph that silently picks one of three possible targets is worse than one that admits it does not know.

glossary.short: Abstract Syntax Tree — the tree-shaped representation of code's grammatical structure that parsers produce.
glossary.long: M03 is entirely about this.

glossary.short: GitHub's extensible text editor (2014–2022).
glossary.long: tree-sitter was built to give it fast, accurate syntax highlighting; the editor is gone, the parser became an industry standard.

glossary.short: An OKF concept documenting the sanctioned, checkable WAY to compute a value — not just what the value means.
glossary.long: The code path or query that produces the value, as distinct from prose describing what the value means — the single source of truth for a governed metric.

glossary.short: A graph metric scoring how often a node sits on shortest paths between other nodes — the god-node detector from M01.
glossary.long: Computing it exactly requires touching a large share of all vertex-edge combinations.

glossary.short: The count of symbols that transitively depend on this one — every function whose behavior could change if it changes.
glossary.long: You computed it with BFS over the reverse index in M01.

glossary.short: BFS: explore a graph level by level from a starting node, using a queue and a visited-set so nothing is processed twice.
Markdown links whose target is a path inside the bundle (e.g.
glossary.long: /services/customer-service.md). They connect concepts regardless of where the described code lives in the actual repo tree.

glossary.short: A family of graph measures scoring how "important" a node is — by how many edges it has (degree), or how many shortest paths run through it (betweenness).
Fixed-size text segments, typically 256–1000 tokens, cut from documents so each piece fits an embedding model's input and stays "focused."
When a conversation outgrows the context window, older content is summarized or dropped.
glossary.long: Files the agent read earlier vanish from it, and re-consulting them means re-reading them at full price.

glossary.short: The fixed amount of text (measured in tokens) a model can consider at once — every file it reads, every instruction, every previous message counts against it.
glossary.long: The prompt, every file it has read, every command output and its own responses all share the one budget.

glossary.short: A vector of hundreds of floats representing the text's meaning; texts with similar meaning get vectors that sit near each other.
A fact read directly out of the source. The graph saw it.
glossary.long: The strongest provenance tag: a call, an import or a definition the parser found in the text. If it is wrong, the code is wrong.

glossary.short: SQLite's built-in Full-Text Search extension (version 5): tokenizes text into an index so "which rows mention X" is answered without scanning every row.
Additional working directories attached to the same repository, letting parallel work happen on different branches without re-cloning.
A node so widely depended on that it distorts everything around it.
glossary.long: The course's example is Registry.lookup with 1,192 callers. Not automatically a bug — some hubs are deliberate. Centrality finds them; judgement decides what to do.

glossary.short: A data structure made of nodes (things) and edges (relationships between pairs of things).
glossary.long: Nothing more exotic than that.

glossary.short: A fact the pipeline derived rather than read. Fallible on purpose.
glossary.long: Dynamic dispatch, reflection and framework wiring produce edges nobody wrote down. Keeping them tagged is what lets a reader discount them.

glossary.short: A minimal convention for sending named method calls with parameters as JSON, and getting results back as JSON.
glossary.long: No REST endpoints, no URLs — just method + params over a pipe.

glossary.short: A background process implementing the Language Server Protocol (LSP) — the same thing that powers go-to-definition in VS Code.
glossary.long: It maintains a live semantic index of a codebase — definitions, references, types. rust-analyzer and pyright are the reference implementations; editors use it for go-to-definition, and agents can too.

glossary.short: The community-detection algorithm used to cluster the graph.
glossary.long: Partitions nodes into densely-connected neighbourhoods, so a codebase can be described by its regions rather than file by file.

glossary.short: A graph-clustering algorithm (successor to Louvain) that partitions nodes to maximize modularity — the degree to which clusters are internally dense and externally sparse.
glossary.long: M01 introduced it.

glossary.short: An automated checker that enforces rules stricter than the format requires — e.g., "every concept must have a description" or "no dangling links." The okf CLI ships 13 built-in lint rules (M07).
Karpathy's April 2026 thought experiment: instead of a model re-searching raw documents on every query, let it build and maintain a living, cross-linked Markdown wiki as durable external memory.
The rungs M03 climbs when a bare name has more than one candidate.
glossary.long: Heuristic name matching first, then LSP-backed disambiguation via textDocument/definition, then accept AMBIGUOUS. Each rung costs more and resolves more, and stopping early is what produces a wrong edge rather than an honest one.

glossary.short: The lightweight plain-text formatting language used in READMEs everywhere: # for headings, [text](url) for links, | pipes | for tables.
glossary.long: Renders natively on GitHub.

glossary.short: Model Context Protocol — the open standard that lets AI assistants call external tools.
glossary.long: A client — the AI assistant — discovers and calls tools a server process exposes, usually over stdio: named JSON messages in, results out. M09 builds a graph-serving MCP server from scratch.

glossary.short: A Model Context Protocol server — a small process exposing typed tools (here: graph queries) to any MCP-aware agent over stdio.
A score measuring how much denser connections are inside clusters than you'd expect by random chance.
glossary.long: High modularity = crisp subsystems.

glossary.short: The stored vectors closest to the query vector by cosine similarity — the mathematical stand-in for "most related text."
A modern fork of the Vim editor.
glossary.long: Its syntax highlighting and code navigation are powered by tree-sitter grammars.

glossary.short: A published OKF implementation the course cites for its benchmark numbers.
glossary.long: Referenced for its ~400x per-query structural-lookup figure, quoted as somebody else's measurement rather than this course's.

glossary.short: OKF: Google Cloud's June 2026 spec for knowledge as a directory of Markdown files with YAML frontmatter.
glossary.long: Track 3 of this course (M06–M08) covers it in depth.

glossary.short: The top-level agent that decomposes a task and dispatches sub-agents.
glossary.long: It decides what context each sub-agent receives — which makes it the gatekeeper of the token budget.

glossary.short: The sample project the whole course runs on.
glossary.long: A small Python service repo — billing, orders, notifications and shared auth — chosen because it is big enough to have real structure and small enough to hold in your head while you check the graph's answers.

glossary.short: A consumption pattern: start at the root index, follow links only as deep as the task requires, and load only the concept files actually needed — instead of loading the entire bundle into context.
Providers cache the processed prefix of a prompt.
glossary.long: If your next request starts with the identical prefix, that part is nearly free. One changed byte early in the prompt invalidates everything after it.

glossary.short: Where a fact in the graph came from, recorded alongside it.
glossary.long: Every edge is either read from the code or derived from it, and the graph says which. A graph that cannot tell you how it knows something is a graph you cannot act on.

glossary.short: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: retrieve relevant text from your own data and paste it into the model's prompt so it can answer from your knowledge instead of its training data.
The W3C semantic-web standards for formal knowledge graphs: typed relationships, machine-checkable ontologies, logical inference.
glossary.long: Far more rigorous than Markdown links — and far heavier to author and maintain.

glossary.short: A markdown file under .claude/skills/ with a name and description in frontmatter.
glossary.long: The agent loads it only when the description matches the task, or when invoked explicitly as a slash command.

glossary.short: A git feature (2.25+) that writes only chosen directories to disk while keeping the rest in the index — a partial working copy of a full repository.
A written standard describing exactly what a valid artifact looks like, so independent tools can produce and consume it interchangeably.
glossary.long: A spec is a contract, not software.

glossary.short: The embedded, serverless SQL database that lives in a single file — no server process, no configuration.
glossary.long: The most deployed database on earth.

glossary.short: The gap between what the graph says and what the code now does.
glossary.long: A knowledge graph is a cache over a moving repository. The question is never whether it goes stale but how fast you notice.

glossary.short: Standard input/output — the server is a subprocess; the client writes requests to its stdin and reads responses from its stdout.
glossary.long: No network, no ports, no auth to configure.

glossary.short: A worker agent with its own separate context window.
glossary.long: It performs a delegated task (like exploration) and returns only a summary to the main conversation; everything it read stays in its context and is discarded.

glossary.short: The standing instructions loaded at the start of every turn — identity, rules, conventions.
glossary.long: Static by design.

glossary.short: The unit LLMs read and bill by; ~4 characters of English/code on average.
glossary.long: “authentication” is about 3 tokens; a 500-line source file about 2,000, and a 24KB file roughly 6,000.

glossary.short: The JSON schemas describing every tool the agent can call.
glossary.long: Loaded whether or not the tools get used.

glossary.short: The parser that turns source files into syntax trees.
glossary.long: Fast, incremental, and grammar-driven per language — which is why the pipeline can re-parse only what changed instead of the whole repository.

glossary.short: Weekly Active Users — the course's stand-in for knowledge the code does not contain.
glossary.long: Used as the example of tribal knowledge: the graph can show you where WAU is computed, but not that it excludes testers on purpose. That part lives in people's heads, and is what documentation is for.

glossary.short: A block of key: value metadata at the very top of a Markdown file, fenced by two lines containing only ---.
glossary.long: YAML is the human-friendly config syntax used by tools like GitHub Actions.
